figures.caption: Table 7: Representation controls across all six attack detectors (test splits). BMP and canonical PNG re-encoding rule out compression, file-size, and encoder-specific metadata cues; grayscale, downsample, and social-media probes test robustness under content-preserving transformations. 𝑎Downsample to 256 × 256, upsample back to 512 × 512 (Lanczos). 𝑏JPEGQ75, resize to 80%, JPEGQ85, resize back.

Table 8: Per-detector reliability statistics on the test split. FP counts use ⌈𝑛clean · FPR⌉; intervals are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 test-set resamples. TPR values are percentages, and smaller clean test sets explain the wider intervals at 0.1% FPR.

Figure 8: Visual comparison across five removal attacks. Top row: clean images. Bottom row: corresponding attacked outputs. All five pipelines—WatermarkAttacker [45], CtrlRegen+ [26], NFPA [32], Boundary Leakage [25], and WiTS [43]—preserve visual quality while leaving forensically detectable processing traces (see Table 3).

Figure 3: Visual comparison of clean images (left) and UnMarker [23]-processed versions (right). The removal pipeline preserves visual quality yet leaves subtle processing traces that a trained detector separates nearly perfectly.

Figure 6: Per-attack spectral fingerprints. Log-ratio of azimuthally averaged attack-residual PSD to content-matched control for all six removers (𝑁 = 5,000 comparisons per attack except Boundary Leakage, 𝑁 = 4,997). Red shading indicates frequencies where the attack adds energy; blue indicates suppression. The zero-crossing frequency (annotated where present) separates the two types of modifications. UnMarker [23] is the only attack with substantial low-frequency excess; the remaining five are dominated by suppression across the full spectrum.

Figure 5: Detection sensitivity by post-processing operator. TPR at FPR = 0.1% and 1% for each tampering operation applied after UnMarker processing [23]. Geometric and colorspace edits preserve detectability; smoothing and compression reduce it, with bilateral filtering as the hardest case.

Figure 10: 2D spectral deviationmaps for all six attacks. Element-wise log-ratio of 2D PSD of attack residuals to content-matched control, with per-attack color scaling. Red indicates excess energy; blue indicates suppression. WatermarkAttacker [45], CtrlRegen+ [26], and Boundary Leakage [25] show cardinal-axis suppression from the diffusion decoder’s convolutional architecture. UnMarker [23] shows isotropic low-frequency excess. NFPA [32] shows a periodic grid from blockwise inversion. WiTS [43] shows mild suppression with decoder-like axis structure.

Figure 9: Visual examples of post-processing operators applied to images. Each column shows one of ten editing operations; rows show three examples. All operators are applied identically to both clean and attacked classes in our tampered evaluation set. Bilateral filtering, non-local means, and aggressive compression substantially modify pixel structure (see Figure 5).
